The **Doomsday Clock** is a symbol that represents the estimated likelihood of a human-made [global catastrophe](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_catastrophic_risk "Global catastrophic risk"), in the opinion of the [nonprofit organization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization") *[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulletin_of_the_Atomic_Scientists "Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists")*.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Maintained since 1947, the Clock is a proxy mechanism for threats to humanity from unchecked scientific and technological advances: A hypothetical global catastrophe is represented by midnight on the Clock, with the *Bulletin's* opinion on how close the world is to "zero" represented by a certain number of minutes or seconds to midnight. This is assessed in January of each year. The main factors influencing the Clock are [nuclear warfare](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_warfare "Nuclear warfare"), [climate change](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), and [artificial intelligence](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) The *Bulletin*'s Science and Security Board monitors new developments in the [life sciences](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_sciences "Life sciences") and technology that could inflict irrevocable harm to humanity.[[4]](#cite_note-2007PressRelease-4)

The Clock's original setting in 1947 was seven minutes to midnight. It has since been set backward eight times and forward 19 times. The farthest time from midnight was 17 minutes in 1991, and the closest is 85 seconds in 2026.[[5]](#cite_note-Lukiv2025-5)

The Clock was moved to 150 seconds (2 minutes, 30 seconds) in 2017, then forward to two minutes to midnight in 2018, and left unchanged in 2019.[[6]](#cite_note-bulletin2019-6) It was moved forward to 100 seconds (1 minute, 40 seconds) in 2020,[[7]](#cite_note-james-7) 90 seconds (1 minute, 30 seconds) in 2023,[[8]](#cite_note-bulletin2023-8) 89 seconds (1 minute, 29 seconds) in 2025,[[9]](#cite_note-:1-9) and 85 seconds (1 minute, 25 seconds) in 2026.[[10]](#cite_note-:2-10)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Bulletin_Atomic_Scientists_Cover.jpg/250px-Bulletin_Atomic_Scientists_Cover.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulletin_Atomic_Scientists_Cover.jpg)

Cover of the 1947 *Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists* issue, featuring the Doomsday Clock at "seven minutes to midnight"

The Doomsday Clock's origin can be traced to the international group of researchers called the Chicago Atomic Scientists, who had participated in the [Manhattan Project](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project").[[11]](#cite_note-The_Spokesman-Review-11) After the [atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki"), they began publishing a [mimeographed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimeograph "Mimeograph") newsletter and then the magazine, *Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists*, which, since its inception, has depicted the Clock on every cover. The Clock was first represented in 1947, when the *Bulletin* co-founder Hyman Goldsmith asked artist [Martyl Langsdorf](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martyl_Langsdorf "Martyl Langsdorf") (wife of Manhattan Project research associate and [Szilárd petition](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szilárd_petition "Szilárd petition") signatory [Alexander Langsdorf Jr.](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Langsdorf_Jr. "Alexander Langsdorf Jr.")) to design a cover for the magazine's June 1947 issue. As [Eugene Rabinowitch](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Rabinowitch "Eugene Rabinowitch"), another co-founder of the *Bulletin*, explained later:

> The *Bulletin*'s Clock is not a gauge to register the ups and downs of the international power struggle; it is intended to reflect basic changes in the level of continuous danger in which mankind lives in the nuclear age...[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Langsdorf chose a clock to reflect the urgency of the problem: like a countdown, the Clock suggests that destruction will naturally occur unless someone takes action to stop it.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

**Stockholm International Peace Research Institute** (**SIPRI**) is an international [institute](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute "Institute") based in [Stockholm](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"), Sweden. It was founded in 1966[[1]](#cite_note-1) and provides data, analysis and recommendations for armed conflict, military expenditure and arms trade as well as disarmament and arms control. The research is based on open sources and is directed to decision-makers, researchers, media and the interested public.

SIPRI's organizational purpose is to conduct scientific research in issues on conflict and cooperation of importance for international peace and security, with the goal of contributing to an understanding for the conditions for a peaceful solution of international conflicts and sustainable peace.

SIPRI was ranked among the top three non-US world-wide think tanks in 2014 by the [University of Pennsylvania](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania") [Lauder Institute](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauder_Institute "Lauder Institute")'s *Global Go To Think Tanks Report*.[[2]](#cite_note-2) In 2020, SIPRI ranked 34th amongst [think tanks](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Think_tank "Think tank") globally.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/ARB-Alva-Myrdal.jpg/250px-ARB-Alva-Myrdal.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ARB-Alva-Myrdal.jpg)

Ambassador Alva Myrdal

In 1964, [Prime Minister of Sweden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Sweden "Prime Minister of Sweden") [Tage Erlander](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tage_Erlander "Tage Erlander") put forward the idea of establishing a peace research institute to commemorate Sweden's 150 years of unbroken peace.

A Swedish Royal Commission chaired by Ambassador [Alva Myrdal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alva_Myrdal "Alva Myrdal") proposed in its 1966 report to establish an institute, later named the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, SIPRI. The institute's research should seek to contribute to "the understanding of the preconditions for a stable peace and for peaceful solutions of international conflicts" and the Commission recommended that research be concentrated on armaments, their limitation and reduction, and [arms control](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_control "Arms control"). The commission also recommended that SIPRI work is of "an applied research character directed towards practical-political questions [which] should be carried on in a constant interchange with research of a more theoretical kind".

SIPRI has built its reputation and standing on competence, professional skills, and the collection of hard data and precise facts, rendering accessible impartial information on weapon developments, arms transfers and production, military expenditure, as well as on arms limitations, reductions and disarmament. The task of the institute is to conduct "scientific research on questions of conflict and cooperation of importance for international peace and security with the aim of contributing to an understanding of the conditions for peaceful solution of international conflicts and for a stable peace".

The Swedish [Riksdag](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riksdag "Riksdag") decided that the Institute be established on 1 July 1966 with the legal status of an independent foundation.

SIPRI's organisation consists of a governing board, director, deputy director, research staff collegium and support staff. The governing board takes decisions on important matters concerning the research agenda, activities, organisation and financial administration of the institute. Other matters are decided by the director. The research staff collegium advises the Director on research matters.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/SIPRI_building.jpg/250px-SIPRI_building.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SIPRI_building.jpg)

SIPRI headquarters in Solna, Stockholm

I have used my 6 calls. The Doomsday Clock jumped from 100s (2020) to 90s in 2023 — a year-over-year move closer to midnight. This is a critical data point. Let me synthesize.

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 1B.10 Research Note

**Lens:** 1B.10 — Did the ruler leave the country's existential-risk posture safer or more dangerous than they inherited it?

**Headline assessment:** On the dominant year-over-year existential-risk metric — the **Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists Doomsday Clock** — 2023 ended **more dangerous** than it began. The clock was set at 100 seconds to midnight in 2020, where it remained through 2022. In **January 2023**, the Bulletin moved the clock to **90 seconds to midnight**, citing the war in Ukraine, modernization of nuclear arsenals, "heightened nuclear rhetoric," and reduced diplomatic engagement on risk reduction. This is the closest setting in the clock's history at that point (a level further escalated to 89 seconds in 2025 and 85 seconds in 2026). On a multi-year comparison, the Doomsday Clock was at 100 seconds when Biden took office in Jan 2021 and at 90 seconds at the end of 2023 — a net worsening of the formal existential-risk metric during his tenure to date. On net-net, however, this lens requires weighing specific 2023 actions: Biden's **AI EO (Oct 30, 2023)**, **cybersecurity strategy**, **biosafety EO**, and **Biden–Xi APEC channel reactivation** are concrete improvements in the institutional risk-reduction infrastructure; while **New START collapse (Feb 21, 2023)**, **AUKUS precedent (Mar 13, 2023)**, **JCPOA stalemate**, and **Israel–Hamas regional escalation** worsened specific risks. The aggregate net effect is closer to neutral or slightly negative on year-over-year 2023 risk posture.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Doomsday Clock moved to 90 seconds to midnight in January 2023 (closest in history)

- **Title / source:** Doomsday Clock
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (citing Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists Science and Security Board statements)
- **Date:** Clock moved to 90 seconds on January 24, 2023 (the article says 2023; specific date cited in Bulletin press release)
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomsday_Clock
- **Summary:** The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists moved the Doomsday Clock to 90 seconds to midnight in January 2023, the closest setting in the clock's history at that point (later moved to 89 seconds in 2025 and 85 seconds in 2026). The Bulletin cited "the war in Ukraine and the risk of nuclear escalation, the breakdown of arms-control agreements, the modernization of nuclear arsenals, the increased risk of a nuclear war, and the deliberate disregard of risk-reduction measures by major powers." The clock remained at 90 seconds throughout 2023 — it was not moved closer or further when the Bulletin reassessed in early 2024. The clock had been at 100 seconds (1 minute 40 seconds) from 2020 through 2022.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working against 1B.10 — formal existential-risk metric worsened during Biden's tenure, including through 2023)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 1B.8, 8B.4, 8B.6

### Claim 2 — Year-over-year 2023 risk trajectory: declined (more dangerous) on multiple dimensions

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across multiple dimensions, 2023 ended more dangerous than it began: (a) Russia suspended New START on Feb 21, ending the last bilateral strategic-arms inspection regime — a transparency/predictability regression; (b) Iran's nuclear program advanced to 60% U-235 enrichment (close to weapons-grade) and Iran restricted IAEA inspector access at Natanz and Fordow in 2023 — a proliferation regression; (c) China continued its nuclear arsenal buildup with SIPRI reporting that China possessed ~410 warheads in Jan 2023 vs ~290 in Jan 2022 (an expansion of ~120 warheads in a single year); (d) Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping (Oct 19 onward) created a new regional escalation vector; (e) Israel–Hamas war (Oct 7 onward) created the highest Middle East crisis risk in decades; (f) the Doomsday Clock remained at 90 seconds — a worsening of the institutional existential-risk metric.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working against 1B.10 — multiple risk dimensions worsened in 2023)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.8

### Claim 3 — Year-over-year 2023 risk trajectory: improved on several dimensions

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across several dimensions, 2023 ended safer than it began: (a) AI Executive Order 14110 (Oct 30, 2023) institutionalized the most comprehensive AI-safety governance by any government, explicitly covering CBRN risks; (b) July 2023 Voluntary AI Commitments from 15 leading AI firms created a baseline of safety, security, and trust commitments with public transparency; (c) March 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy rebalanced responsibility toward defenders and signaled regulatory baselines for critical-infrastructure operators; (d) April 11, 2023 Biosafety EO expanded review of dual-use research of concern; (e) Biden–Xi APEC meeting (Nov 15, 2023) reactivated mil-to-mil communication channels that had been suspended for months; (f) Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023) — a multinational coalition response to Houthi attacks — preserved freedom of navigation and reduced escalation risk; (g) NATO expansion (Finland joined Apr 4, 2023; Sweden Mar 2024) extended the alliance's territorial depth.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working for 1B.10 — several institutional risk-reduction improvements)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.7, 1B.9

### Claim 4 — SIPRI 2023 nuclear arsenals data

- **Title / source:** SIPRI Yearbook 2023 / SIPRI 2023 nuclear arsenals press release
- **Publisher:** SIPRI / Wikipedia
- **Date:** Released June 12, 2023 (SIPRI Yearbook); covers Jan 2023 snapshot
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIPRI (and combined evidence)
- **Summary:** SIPRI's Yearbook 2023, released in June 2023, reported the global nuclear arsenal count as of January 2023: approximately 12,512 warheads worldwide, of which about 9,576 were in military stockpiles for potential use. The United States maintained approximately 5,244 warheads (with ~1,550 deployed); Russia held ~5,889 (largest arsenal); China had expanded to ~410 warheads, up from ~290 in Jan 2022 (the largest single-year expansion in SIPRI's records); India ~164; Pakistan ~170; France ~290; UK ~225; Israel ~90; North Korea ~30. The SIPRI assessment noted that "the risks of nuclear weapons being used are higher than at any time since the height of the Cold War." China was a particular concern: SIPRI noted that China was engaged in a "significant expansion" of its nuclear arsenal and might have 1,000 warheads by 2030 if the trend continued.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working against 1B.10 — net global nuclear arsenal expansion in 2023, especially China's)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.5, 8B.4

### Claim 5 — AUKUS submarine deal (Mar 13, 2023): precedent for nuclear-propulsion technology transfer to non-NPT state

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Mar 13, 2023 San Diego announcement
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** The AUKUS "optimal pathway" announced Mar 13, 2023 in San Diego committed the U.S. to transfer Virginia-class SSNs (nuclear-powered attack submarines) to Australia and to begin rotational basing of U.S./UK SSNs in Australia. This required a bespoke IAEA Article 14 arrangement and U.S. legislation. Critics argued the deal set a precedent that lowered the bar for other non-NPT states to seek similar arrangements; proponents argued it strengthens deterrence against China without weakening non-proliferation. From a year-over-year risk perspective, AUKUS marginally weakened the non-proliferation norm even as it strengthened the U.S.-Australia-UK alliance.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working against 1B.10 — precedent-setting proliferation-adjacent transfer)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 6 — Biden–Xi APEC meeting (Nov 15, 2023) reactivated crisis-communication channels

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024 (reflecting Nov 15, 2023 event)
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** At the APEC summit in San Francisco on Nov 15, 2023, Biden met Xi Jinping — their first face-to-face in a year. The meeting reportedly included the resumption of military-to-military communication channels (agreed at Bali G20 in Nov 2022 but not implemented) and nuclear-strategic-stability language. The channel-preservation outcome was concrete: mil-to-mil communications restarted, fentanyl-cooperation talks advanced. This is a year-over-year risk-reduction step in U.S.–China relations.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working for 1B.10 — risk-reduction channel reactivation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.8, 8B.4

### Claim 7 — Chinese balloon incident (Jan 28 – Feb 4, 2023): textbook de-escalation by delay

- **Title / source:** 2023 Chinese balloon incident
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** January 28 – February 4, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Chinese_balloon_incident
- **Summary:** A high-altitude Chinese balloon entered U.S. airspace on Jan 28, 2023, transited Alaska, western Canada, and the contiguous United States over six days. Biden delayed the shoot-down for ~6 days, despite domestic pressure to act immediately, because the overland shoot-down risked harm to civilians on the ground; the U.S. shot it down on Feb 4 over U.S. territorial waters off South Carolina. The response was calibrated and channels with China preserved; Blinken postponed a planned Beijing trip rather than escalating; the eventual Nov 15 Biden–Xi APEC meeting reactivated mil-to-mil communications.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working for 1B.10 — crisis-management de-escalation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.5, 1B.8, 8B.4

### Claim 8 — AI Executive Order 14110 (Oct 30, 2023): most comprehensive AI governance by any government

- **Title / source:** Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (citing Federal Register 2023-24283)
- **Date:** Signed October 30, 2023; rescinded January 20, 2025
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_on_Safe,_Secure,_and_Trustworthy_Artificial_Intelligence
- **Summary:** Executive Order 14110 was the most comprehensive AI governance by any government, requiring federal agencies to create dedicated "chief artificial intelligence officer" positions and invoking the Defense Production Act for frontier-model safety. The order explicitly directs DOE and DHS to "address AI systems' threats to critical infrastructure, as well as chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cybersecurity risks." This is a year-over-year improvement in the institutional risk-reduction infrastructure for AI/CBRN existential risks.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working for 1B.10 — institutional risk-reduction infrastructure improvement)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.3, 1B.7, 1B.9, 8B.7

### Claim 9 — Hur classified-documents incident: a direct contradiction of the safety-of-custody lens

- **Title / source:** Joe Biden classified documents incident
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Incident timeline Nov 2022 – Feb 2024; key 2023 milestones Jan–June 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_classified_documents_incident
- **Summary:** Between November 2022 and June 2023, Biden's attorneys discovered at least six batches of classified government documents — totaling between 25 and 30 documents — in three locations: Penn Biden Center, Wilmington home, University of Delaware. The documents dated to his Senate tenure and vice presidency and included intelligence briefings on Ukraine, Iran, and the United Kingdom. The Hur special counsel investigation ran Jan 12, 2023 – Mar 11, 2024; the Feb 8, 2024 report found "willful retention" but declined prosecution. This is a direct year-over-year institutional risk to U.S. nuclear commander custody discipline.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working against 1B.10 — institutional risk reduction regressed)
- **Also informs:** 1B.3, 1B.7, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 10 — Israel–Hamas war (Oct 7 onward) and Houthi Red Sea crisis (Oct 19 onward): regional escalation in Q4 2023

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy / Red Sea crisis / Israel–Hamas war
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** Oct 7 onward
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel (killing ~1,200 Israelis, taking ~250 hostages) and Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza (with massive civilian casualties) created the worst Middle East crisis risk in decades. Iran's proxy network expanded the crisis (Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping Oct 19; Iraqi militia attacks on U.S. forces). Biden's response was "blank check" political backing for Israel plus calibrated coalition response (Operation Prosperity Guardian, Dec 18, 2023) — but the regional crisis worsened through Q4 2023, with risk of further escalation.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working against 1B.10 — Q4 2023 regional escalation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 1B.8, 8B.4, 8B.6

### Claim 11 — Domestic U.S. institutional risk factors in 2023

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Domestic institutional risk factors in 2023 included: (a) Hur classified-documents investigation raising questions about the U.S. nuclear commander's fitness; (b) Senate rejection of Biden's judicial and executive nominees due to Sen. Tuberville's (R-AL) holds on military promotions (a record 300+ holds in 2023) — which critics argued weakened military leadership continuity including in nuclear-relevant commands; (c) House Republican opening of impeachment inquiry into Biden (Dec 13, 2023) — political polarization adding uncertainty to U.S. governance continuity. None of these directly destabilized nuclear command-and-control in 2023, but they raised institutional risk.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working against 1B.10 — institutional risk factors in 2023)
- **Also informs:** 1B.3, 7B.6, 8B.3

### Claim 12 — Bilateral arms control collapsed in 2023 (New START suspension Feb 21, 2023)

- **Title / source:** New START
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Feb 21, 2023 suspension
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START
- **Summary:** Russia suspended New START participation on Feb 21, 2023, ending all on-site inspections and data exchanges. The treaty — the last bilateral strategic-arms limit — ultimately expired Feb 5, 2026 with no replacement. The 2023 suspension was a year-over-year regression in arms-control infrastructure.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.10 (working against 1B.10 — bilateral arms-control collapse)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 1B.8

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 1B.10

- **Doomsday Clock moved to 90 seconds in 2023** — closest setting in history at that point, holding through 2023.
- **New START collapse (Feb 21, 2023)** — last bilateral strategic-arms inspection regime ended.
- **Iran nuclear program advanced** — 60% enrichment and reduced IAEA access.
- **China nuclear buildup** — ~120-warhead year-over-year expansion.
- **AUKUS precedent** — non-proliferation norm weakened.
- **JCPOA stalemate** — no Iranian non-proliferation framework restored.
- **Hur classified-documents incident** — institutional custody-discipline failure.
- **Israel–Hamas and Houthi crises (Q4 2023)** — regional escalation vectors.
- **CTBT not ratified** — test-moratorium regime remains on voluntary basis.
- **Sentinel ICBM 81% cost overrun** — modernization fiscal stress.

## Favorable evidence on 1B.10

- **AI EO 14110 (Oct 30, 2023)** — most comprehensive AI governance by any government; explicit CBRN safeguards.
- **July 2023 Voluntary AI Commitments** — 15 leading AI firms signed.
- **March 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy** — rebalanced responsibility toward defenders.
- **April 2023 Biosafety EO** — institutional review of dual-use research.
- **Biden–Xi APEC meeting (Nov 15, 2023)** — mil-to-mil channel reactivation.
- **Chinese balloon de-escalation by delay** — calibrated crisis response.
- **Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023)** — coalition Red Sea response, restrained.
- **NATO expansion (Finland Apr 4, 2023)** — alliance territorial depth extended.
- **Biden–Xi mil-to-mil communication restoration** — concrete channel preservation.
- **Ukraine cluster munitions framing** — risk-reduction justification.
- **Continued sanctions enforcement on adversaries.**
- **No 2023 nuclear incident or unauthorized launch.**
- **Continued 1992 nuclear-test moratorium.**
- **No domestic repression, no martial law.**

## Net assessment

The net effect of Biden's 2023 actions on U.S. existential-risk posture is **slightly negative** on the dominant year-over-year metric (Doomsday Clock at 90s vs 100s at start of 2023), but **mixed overall**. The institutional risk-reduction infrastructure (AI EO, cybersecurity strategy, biosafety EO, mil-to-mil channels, NATO expansion) is materially stronger than at the start of the year; the strategic-arms control and non-proliferation infrastructure (New START collapse, JCPOA stalemate, AUKUS precedent) is materially weaker; and the regional risk environment (Israel-Hamas, Houthi, Russia-Ukraine grinding war) is materially worse. The dominant single fact is the Doomsday Clock at 90 seconds — the closest setting in history at that point — which on balance represents a slight worsening of U.S. existential-risk posture during 2023.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Specific 2023 SIPRI Yearbook details** — only summary available.
  - **The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists' specific Jan 2023 statement** — only summary here.
  - **Specific 2023 Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI) reports** — NTI publishes annual Nuclear Security Index but the 2023 details are not directly captured.
  - **Detailed 2023 Iranian nuclear-program IAEA quarterly reports** — public but not directly retrieved.
  - **Specific 2023 Chinese nuclear-expansion numbers** — only summary captured.
  - **The 2023 Global Catastrophic Risks report from various organizations** — Cambridge Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, Future of Life Institute, Centre for the Governance of AI — public but not directly captured.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the Jan 24, 2023 Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists' statement on the Doomsday Clock, (b) the SIPRI Yearbook 2023 specific arsenal numbers, (c) the IAEA Director General's quarterly Iran reports for 2023, (d) the NTI 2023 Nuclear Security Index, and (e) the 2023 Global Catastrophic Risks Landscape report.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 1B.10 is the **Doomsday Clock movement to 90 seconds to midnight** — the closest setting in history at that point. This metric, combined with the New START suspension, JCPOA stalemate, AUKUS precedent, Iran nuclear advancement, China nuclear buildup, Israel–Hamas regional escalation, and Hur classified-documents incident, points to a **net slightly negative year-over-year risk trajectory** in 2023, partially offset by AI EO 14110, July 2023 Voluntary AI Commitments, March 2023 cybersecurity strategy, April 2023 biosafety EO, Biden–Xi APEC channel reactivation, and NATO expansion. The AI EO 14110 is the strongest single favorable item; the Doomsday Clock at 90 seconds is the strongest single unfavorable item.
